clue.text: Parting buttocks audibly

indicators.note: audibly says the word for buttocks is heard spoken, giving its twin in sound but not in spelling

parts.note: the breech is the backside or buttocks, as in a breech birth

explanation.surface: A cheeky description of the cleft between someone's buttocks, said out loud.
explanation.definitionFit: A breach is a gap, split or break-up, so it means a parting, whether of walls or of friends.

clue.text: Right time to put on pants and woad?

indicators.note: pants are put on around the body, so the rubbish word is wrapped around the other pieces

parts.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, as is duff
right, as an acknowledgement, means yes

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether it is the proper moment to pull on trousers and daub on blue woad, ancient-Briton style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pants' looks like trousers but is British slang meaning rubbish, and 'to put on' treats it as clothing wrapped round the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Woad is a plant-based blue colouring, an example of a substance used for dyeing; the question mark flags definition by example.

clue.text: Decrepit old man's boob

parts.note: old man is slang for father, PA, here with the possessive S
boob is slang for a breast, as is tit

explanation.surface: A crude remark about an elderly man's breast, or perhaps his blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boob' could mean a mistake, but here it is the slang word for a breast.
explanation.definitionFit: Being past it is an idiom for being too old or worn out to function, which is what decrepit describes.

clue.text: Expressionless bloody monster

parts.note: bloody and dead are both British intensifiers meaning very, as in 'dead good'
to monster is informal British for criticising severely, which is also to pan

explanation.surface: A blood-soaked creature that shows no emotion on its face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'monster' reads as a noun but is the verb meaning to slate, i.e. PAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A deadpan face or delivery deliberately shows no emotion, so it is impassive or expressionless.

clue.text: Two-part coverage of British couple stopped by relatives

indicators.note: the pair of numerals is plugged in the middle by the family word, as a hole is stopped

parts.note: a couple is two, written in Roman numerals as II
relatives are kin

explanation.surface: News coverage in two parts about a British couple whose family dropped in.
explanation.definitionFit: A bikini is a two-piece swimsuit, so it is coverage, of a sort, in two parts.

clue.text: Good health of two mates, each with a shed

indicators.note: shed means discarded, so each copy of the mate word loses its letter A
two says the mate word appears twice over

parts.note: china is Cockney rhyming slang for mate (china plate)

explanation.surface: Two friends who each own a garden shed raise a toast to one another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a shed' looks like a garden hut, but means the letter A is shed from each CHINA.
explanation.definitionFit: Chin-chin is an old-fashioned drinking toast, like 'cheers' or 'your good health'.

clue.text: Vagrant grew teary, consequence of having bath?

indicators.note: vagrant means wandering, so the letters wander into a new order

explanation.surface: A tramp became tearful, perhaps from the novelty of a bath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vagrant' looks like a noun for the person crying, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Grey water is used household wastewater, such as what is left in the tub after bathing.

clue.text: Terse husband gripped by shame

indicators.note: the husband's letter is held inside the word for shame

parts.note: 'what a shame' means 'what a pity'

explanation.surface: A curt husband is held in the grip of embarrassment.
explanation.definitionFit: Pithy remarks are brief and to the point, so they are concise or terse.

clue.text: Lads use it, suffering lethargy

indicators.note: suffering suggests being hurt or knocked about, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Lads use something while laid low by tiredness.
explanation.definitionFit: Lassitude is physical or mental weariness, a near synonym for listlessness.

clue.text: Northerners and fellow boozers

parts.note: boozer is British slang for a pub, and inns are pubs

explanation.surface: People from the north and their drinking companions.
explanation.definitionFit: Finland lies in northern Europe, so its people are northerners.

clue.text: Strongly recommend 50% reduction in your wage

indicators.note: cutting each of the two words by half leaves only its latter two letters

explanation.surface: A call to push hard for halving someone's pay.
explanation.definitionFit: To urge is to press or advocate earnestly, so it means strongly recommend.

clue.text: Without any energy, three use tee for drive

indicators.note: E is the physics symbol for energy, and without any means every E is dropped

explanation.surface: A golfer, lacking oomph, uses a tee three times to drive.
explanation.definitionFit: Thrust is forward push or driving force, so it can mean drive as a noun.

clue.text: Look mean, having no weaknesses

parts.note: an air is a look or manner, as in 'an air of confidence'
tight is informal for stingy or mean

explanation.surface: Someone who seems stingy and has no chinks in their armour.
explanation.definitionFit: An airtight argument or alibi has no flaws or loopholes for anyone to exploit.

clue.text: Lord's holding first of enquiries into unruly mid-off

indicators.note: into says the picked letter goes inside the scrambled letters
unruly means disorderly, so the letters are jumbled
first of picks the opening letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A cricket lord fields enquiries about a badly behaved mid-off fielder.
explanation.walkthrough: Mid-off is a fielding position in cricket. 'unruly' rearranges MIDOFF to FIFDOM, and 'into' puts E inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A fief is the land a vassal held from a feudal lord, and a fiefdom is that estate or domain.

clue.text: Manxwoman one defames?

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral
with one as subject, 'one defames' becomes 'I slander', so the verb form matches the first person

explanation.surface: Is a woman from the Isle of Man someone who spreads slander?
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'one defames' as 'I slander'. The Isle of Man lies in the Irish Sea.
explanation.definitionFit: A Manxwoman lives on the Isle of Man, so she is an inhabitant of an island; a definition by example.

clue.text: Loves to pinch scientists roughly

indicators.note: the pair of zeros squeeze the scientists' abbreviation between them

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, O, so two loves are OO
RS is the Royal Society, Britain's academy of scientists

explanation.surface: Lovers set out to rob some scientists, more or less.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Or so' after a number means approximately, as in 'ten or so'.

clue.text: Leader shunning wholesale evidence of misery

indicators.note: the leader is the first letter, and shunning means it is dropped

parts.note: wholesale changes are sweeping changes

explanation.surface: A boss avoids the bulk trade, a sign of unhappiness.
explanation.definitionFit: Crying is an outward sign of sorrow, so weeping is evidence that someone is miserable.

clue.text: Praise extremely powerful reviews

indicators.note: extremely means at the extremes, so only the end letters of the word are used

parts.note: an audit is a formal review of accounts

explanation.surface: Reviews heap tremendously strong praise on something.
explanation.definitionFit: Plaudits are expressions of applause or approval, so they are praise.

clue.text: Name of man embracing love goddess

indicators.note: the man's title wraps around the other pieces as in a hug

parts.note: Mr is the title for a man
love is zero in tennis, O
Nike is the Greek goddess of victory

explanation.surface: A man's name, with him hugging the goddess of love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'love goddess' suggests Venus or Aphrodite, but love is O and the goddess is NIKE.
explanation.definitionFit: A moniker is an informal word for a name or nickname.

clue.text: Duke excluded from king's company outside

indicators.note: the duke's letter is shut out of the king's company

parts.note: Alfred the Great was an English king, so his company is Alfred's Co, CO being short for company

explanation.surface: A duke is shut out from the royal party, left standing outdoors.
explanation.definitionFit: Al fresco, from Italian, means in the open air, so a meal eaten outside.

clue.text: Most weirdly, bats return to natural habitat

indicators.note: bats is slang for crazy, so the letters are scrambled madly
most of a word means all but its last letter

explanation.surface: Bats, behaving very strangely, go back into the wild.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bats' looks like the animals, but is slang for crazy and signals the anagram of WEIRDL.
explanation.definitionFit: To rewild land, or a species, is to restore it to its natural, uncultivated state.

clue.text: Unkempt chap exhausted after long nap

indicators.note: after says the emptied chap comes behind the carpet pile in the answer

parts.note: shag is a fabric or carpet with a long, rough nap or pile

indicators.note: exhausted means emptied, so the middle of the word is removed

parts.note: guy means a chap

explanation.surface: A dishevelled man is worn out after a lengthy snooze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'long nap' suggests a sleep, but nap here is the pile on a fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Shaggy hair is long and untidy, so shaggy means unkempt.

clue.text: Then finally you kiss me, blind drunk

parts.note: so can mean then, as in 'so, what next?'

indicators.note: finally picks the closing letter of each of the four words that follow

explanation.surface: A romantic plea: then you finally kiss me, while utterly drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blind drunk' looks like one phrase, but 'blind' supplies its last letter and 'drunk' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Soused is informal for being drunk, from souse meaning to soak in liquid.

clue.text: Threaten to go out to speak after close of meeting

indicators.note: after puts the speaking word behind the meeting's closing letter
the close of a word is its final letter

parts.note: to utter is to speak

explanation.surface: Someone threatens to walk out and have their say when the meeting ends.
explanation.definitionFit: A candle flame gutters when it flickers and is about to go out.

clue.text: Is aware Primark now sells sandwiches

indicators.note: sandwiches means holds between, so the phrase holds the answer inside it

explanation.surface: Someone is aware that the budget clothing chain Primark has begun selling sandwiches.
explanation.definitionFit: To know something is to be aware of it, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Arachne ultimately got by on £51 in cash

indicators.note: on means placed after, so the setter and the end letters follow the money

parts.note: 51 is LI in Roman numerals, and a pound sterling is a quid
Arachne is the setter, who refers to herself as I

indicators.note: ultimately picks the final letter of each of the two words that follow

explanation.surface: The setter claims to have scraped by on just fifty-one pounds in cash.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter's name in the clue usually stands for I or ME.
explanation.definitionFit: Liquidity is the holding of readily available money, so in finance it means cash or liquid assets.

clue.text: Delivered letter: ending taken to heart

indicators.note: the word's final letter is moved to its centre

parts.note: delta is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A posted letter whose ending was taken to heart by its reader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'letter' suggests mail, but it is the Greek letter DELTA, whose last letter A is moved into the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Dealt means handed out or given, as cards are dealt or a blow delivered.

clue.text: Prime case of extortion following incident in Home Counties

indicators.note: following puts the extortion case letters behind the incident set in the Home Counties
in places the incident between the two letters for the region

parts.note: the Home Counties are the English counties around London, in the South East, SE
an incident is an event

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outer letters

explanation.surface: A top-grade extortion case follows an incident near London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prime' looks like an adjective meaning first-rate, but it is the number type: seventeen has no divisors but itself and one.
explanation.definitionFit: Seventeen is a prime number, divisible only by itself and one, so it is an example of a prime.
